title: The Betrayal of God, of the Faithful and the Mighty (Ecclesiastic Nietzsche)
summary: Part 1 of an Educated Barbarian triptych on Nietzsche and religion (Beyond Good and Evil). NH argues Nietzsche did not hate God: he admired early faith as a freely chosen, painful discipline against instinct, and deplored its later transformation by slave morality into rigid, resentful absolutes. He ends with the 'mystery of the saint': why mighty medieval men bowed to priests, read as a form of will to power.
claims: Nietzsche did not hate God or religion; he saw a reason for its existence and deplored what religion became afterwards
Theologians and religious scholars cannot trace religion's origins because they stop when they have to question established morals, like a hunting dog that freezes once it catches the scent
Atheists who attack religion usually ridicule it broadly without studying its particulars

Examining religion takes a profound and 'bruised' intellect plus a wicked spirituality able to float above morals; intelligence that avoids taboos is useless, and wickedness without intelligence just makes a clown
Following Nietzsche, you must do everything yourself to truly know something; you cannot rely on other people's knowledge
Early Christian faith was a 'continuous suicide of reason': a freely chosen, repeated discipline against one's most basic instincts
Faith works like any discipline: a set of restrictions that must be reaffirmed daily or it withers, because the self keeps trying to revolt
Original faith meant sacrificing part of one's freedom, pride and self-confidence in hope of a return with no guarantee, like putting an apple in a machine that may give it back covered in chocolate
Discipline is pain you accept to avoid a greater pain: regret, not achieving anything, lying to yourself
Faith without pain is not faith; modern watered-down religions that removed everything uncomfortable are empty shells, because you cannot get something for nothing
Modern people read religious texts literally like a newspaper and miss the allegory; God on the cross is an allegory of illogical, absurd acceptance
Modern people judge the past anachronistically and call earlier eras barbaric because they cannot understand other time periods
Freely chosen membership produces more committed members than forced membership, as with a club you are free to leave
Even if religions were divinely dictated, humans modify their texts and interpretations, so they can be corrupted; refusing to admit this leaves you blind to it
Per Nietzsche, the slave classes turned faith into an absolute that could not be left or questioned, as revenge against their masters: a slave revolt in morals
Slave morality inverts values so that the weak, poor and oppressed become the heroes and the strong the villains ('the last will be first')
Escaping one set of chains usually means jumping into another; true liberation is rare
The black-and-white, nuance-free morality we live with today was inherited from degenerated religion
One value for a man is poison to another: refusing to see pain as bad works for the strong but breaks the weak, who want to be protected from pain

Nietzsche attributes the slave revolt in morals to the Jews; NH presents it as a critique of Judaism's moral legacy within Christianity and later religions, and notes that criticism of this kind was common among older authors
Nietzsche's answer to oppression: get strong yourself, rather than poisoning morality by inverting it
Belief in an afterlife grows out of the need to justify present suffering; expecting real life to begin after death breeds resentment of this existence, when the struggle itself is the reward
Fasting or abstinence only works if you understand why you are doing it; without that meaning it rebounds into gluttony or, as with NoFap, a sexual rebound
Trying to cut off sensual inclinations entirely fails because they resurface elsewhere; the goal is to control them, not eliminate them
Mighty medieval kings and warlords bowed to frail priests out of fascination with voluntary privation, the mystery of the saint: a 'will to no will'
Medieval faith was also will to power: serving an infinite God removes the ceiling, which explains the Crusaders' belief that they could fight against huge odds
Will to power is not big muscles or being an alpha; it is a never-satisfied thirst to keep expanding
Faith only makes sense for the strong: self-humiliation means something when humiliation is rare, but modern mediocre men are already humiliated and leashed by government, law and morality
